opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting question, and I'm not sure I have a confident picture. When I think about delegation, I think about the difference between asking a system to do one specific thing, like "write me a paragraph about X," and handing it something more like a goal, like "sort out my travel for this conference," where it has to break the task down, decide what matters, and come back to you only when it actually needs you.

My impression is that these systems have improved a lot at the first kind of thing and are gradually creeping toward the second. The individual pieces are often surprisingly good. What's harder is stringing them together reliably over a longer horizon: noticing when something has gone wrong, not confidently barreling ahead on a bad assumption, knowing which decisions are yours to make and which you should check on. That kind of judgment is a lot of what we mean when we say we trust someone with a task.

I also think it's easy to misjudge progress here in both directions. You see an impressive demo and think, "this can basically run errands for me now," and then you try it on your own messy life and it falls over in some mundane way. Or you see it fail and conclude it's nowhere close, when actually the failure was fairly shallow and fixable. So I try to hold it loosely.

More broadly, this is part of why I'm interested in asking lots of people, including AI researchers, when they expect various capabilities to arrive. Forecasts tend to be quite spread out and quite sensitive to how you phrase the question. "When will AI be able to do this task" and "when will this occupation be automated" can get very different answers, even though they seem logically connected. High-level delegation sits right in that gap. It's the bridge between "can do tasks" and "can do jobs," so I think it's one of the more important things to watch, and one where our intuitions are probably least calibrated.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts handling a specific task with taking a higher-level goal that requires breaking it down, and says competence at individual pieces can still depend on higher-level judgment and user check-ins.

r002.rationale: It describes a delegated goal that would require subtasks, but does not clearly state that ChatGPT can carry them out without the user specifying each one; the response says systems are only gradually moving toward that ability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I find it kind of surprising how little of that has happened, given how impressive the underlying models are. If you'd asked me a few years ago what it would look like once you had a system that could write decent code, answer most factual questions, and hold a coherent conversation about basically anything, I think I would have guessed that we'd pretty quickly be handing it whole tasks. Like, "go deal with my taxes," or "figure out which conference I should go to and book it." And that's mostly not what's happened. People are using it a lot, but overwhelmingly in this very hands-on, back-and-forth way, where you're the one holding the task in your head and it's doing pieces of it.

I've been trying to think about why that is, and I don't think it's just that the models aren't good enough in some raw sense. I think part of it is that delegation requires a kind of reliability that's different from being impressive on average. If I hand something off to a person, I need to trust that if they hit something confusing, they'll come back and ask, or at least not quietly do something strange. And the models are still pretty bad at that. They'll confidently proceed through a situation where a sensible assistant would stop. So you end up having to check everything, and at that point you haven't really delegated, you've just gotten a very fast first draft.

There's also something about the models not having much of a sense of your situation. A lot of what makes delegation work with a human is that they know you, they know the context, they know what you'd want in cases you didn't explicitly specify. The models have to be told all of that every time, and spelling out all of it is often about as much work as just doing the thing.

That said, I do think it's moving. The agentic stuff, where the model takes actions and runs tools over longer stretches, is clearly getting better, and the time horizon of tasks they can handle seems to be growing fairly steadily, at least on the benchmarks people have been tracking. So I don't want to say this is some fundamental barrier. I think it's more that the gap between "can do each step" and "can be trusted with the whole thing" turned out to be larger than I expected, and we're sort of watching it get crossed slowly rather than all at once. Which, honestly, from a safety point of view, I'm somewhat relieved about. It means there's a bit more time to notice what goes wrong when you actually do hand things over.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts handling individual steps with being trusted to manage a whole task, but does not describe autonomy as a nested hierarchy where competence at one level still requires direction from a higher level.

r002.rationale: It does not state that ChatGPT can carry out multiple implicit subtasks within a request, such as writing a letter, without the user specifying them.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s been a pretty substantial shift in what you can delegate. It used to be that getting a computer to do something involved specifying the procedure in quite a lot of detail. With ChatGPT, you can often describe the outcome you want, and it will fill in some of the steps. That seems like an important kind of progress, even when the individual tasks aren’t especially impressive.

But there’s a distinction between being able to do that for a short task and being able to reliably take responsibility for a larger project. If I have to keep checking the output, noticing where it’s gone wrong, and deciding what to ask next, then I’m still doing a lot of the management. The stronger version of delegation would be something like, ‘Here’s what I’m trying to accomplish; work out what needs to happen, and come back when you’ve done it—or when there’s a decision you need me to make.’

So I think ChatGPT is progress in that direction. I’m less sure how much the ability to handle a brief instruction tells us about when it will be able to carry out a long, messy task without supervision. Reliability and knowing when to ask for help seem quite central to that.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes handling a short task from taking responsibility for a larger project, explaining that the user may still need to check progress and direct what happens next.

r002.rationale: It says users can describe the desired outcome and ChatGPT will fill in some steps, communicating that it handles implicit subtasks without each being specified.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a distinction between being able to do a task when someone carefully sets it up for you and being able to take a high-level goal and work out what needs to happen. ChatGPT seems to have made a lot of progress on the first thing. You can delegate quite substantial pieces of work to it, but you often still have to supply the context, break things down, and check whether the result actually makes sense.

The further step is being able to say, “Here’s what I’m trying to accomplish,” and have it handle those intermediate decisions reliably. That involves more than giving a good answer to any particular question. It has to notice when it’s missing information, recover from mistakes, and keep track of the goal over time. I’m uncertain how quickly that will come together, but it seems like an important distinction when thinking about how much work these systems can take over.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes doing a carefully set up task from handling a high-level goal and says the user often still must provide context, break work down, and check results—showing lower-level competence can require higher-level direction.

r002.rationale: It says ChatGPT can handle substantial pieces of work, but does not state that it can perform multiple implicit subtasks within a request such as writing a letter without specifying each one.
